decisions.executionNote: Raise right elbow-up toward the cup's workspace, keeping the cup upright and the left arm parked; geometry differs from reference.

Lift the closed right gripper vertically without tipping; verify cup and balls move with it before transporting.

Lower the left fingers around the narrow vase neck, with small forward motion to center the neck between the jaws.

Test vase retention with a slow vertical lift; keep its mouth upright and cup stationary.

Close fully at the deeper neck grasp, then test with an 18 mm lift; watch the vase rather than the gripper state.
The vase still appears supported by the table. Lower back below its flare and test a very small inward translation to assess engagement.
Release the unretained vase and lower the open left gripper below the wide mouth to its narrower body, keeping the cup still.
Close below the vase flare at the current contact-limited height and test a small lift without further downward force.
Back the left palm away from the flare and lower to the narrower vase body for a less obstructed horizontal grasp.
Close around the lower vase body and test retention with a small lift and inward motion; do not infer a grasp from commanded closure.
Test a slow inward vase translation while maintaining closure and lift; inspect whether the vessel follows rather than assuming retention.
The vase remains fixed in RGB, so stop trying to move it. Clear the left hand and lift the retained cup for a central handover, without crossing arms.
Prepare a central cup handover: raise and orient the open left gripper inward while slowly rotating the retained cup toward the demonstrated safe presentation angle.
Continue the elevated central handover approach. The cup and all visible balls remain retained; keep left fingers open until aligned.
Finish presenting the cup toward the open left hand, with slow rotations to avoid spilling. Keep both elbows up and separated.
Bring the open left fingers around the cup body, approaching slowly while the right rim grasp remains closed.
Close the left hand around the cup body while the right hand continues supporting the rim; do not release the right grasp yet.
Maintain the left body grasp; open and withdraw the right fingers along their insertion direction to verify the handover in RGB.

Transport the left-held cup toward the vase while restoring it upright. Start returning the empty right arm through its own workspace.
Continue carrying the cup leftward above the vase's region while untipping it, and retract the empty right arm gradually.
Position the upright left-held cup above the vase's left side, still elevated for clearance, while continuing the right arm's return.
Align the cup lip over the vase before tipping, accounting for the cup's offset from link6. Finish returning the right hand toward origin.
Begin a slow rightward cup tilt above the vase, keeping the gripper closed and the lip over its opening; inspect before the balls begin to roll out.
Hold the partial tilt while lowering and shifting the cup toward the vase mouth in depth, reducing the drop before pouring.
Increase the cup's tilt slowly toward the vase and make a small lip-position correction, keeping the drop short and watching for the first balls.
Lower the pouring lip slightly and continue tipping toward the vase in small increments, checking ball motion and mouth alignment.
Avoid further contact-limited descent; tip the cup closer to horizontal with a small inward lip correction over the vase, keeping closure commanded.

Move the empty left hand toward a downward inspection of the spilled balls and fallen cup, staying above the vase for clearance.
Continue moving to a clear overhead view of the cup and spilled balls, with the left fingers open and the right arm parked.
Orient the open left fingers vertically above the spilled balls for a possible individual recovery; avoid the vase and fallen cup.
Align vertically over the isolated ball nearest the vase, using the head image and wrist view, with ample height before descent.
Replan after the continuity rejection: retain the near-vertical orientation and lower gradually above the isolated ball, rather than pushing farther forward.
Descend toward the isolated ball with a narrower open jaw and a small lateral correction; inspect at low height before closing.
The descent was obstructed, likely by the vase. Lift and move right to the clear isolated ball, making the fingers fully vertical before another attempt.
After the continuity rejection and large contact residual, open and withdraw upward/backward from the vase before re-approaching any ball.

Avoid further contact-limited descent. Make a small image-based forward correction to the isolated ball and close the narrow jaws for a retention test.
Test the isolated-ball pinch with a slow vertical lift while keeping closure commanded; verify the ball follows the fingers.

Lift the retried pinch slightly upward and backward while maintaining closure, checking whether the isolated ball is retained.
The ball was not retained. Reopen and move the ball farther inside the jaws at the previous low height, without forcing below the contact-limited plane.
The isolated ball is centered inside the narrow jaws. Close fully, then make a short lift to check visual retention.
Move the closed pinch slightly away from the pickup point toward the vase to distinguish a retained ball from one merely occluded by the jaws.
No ball followed the last pinch. Reopen and correct the approach to truly vertical above the isolated ball, accounting for the long finger offset from link6.
The vertical approach is tracking poorly near a wrist limit. Use a shallower approach from behind the ball, keeping the fingertip position approximately aligned as the wrist lowers.
Keep the contact-limited height and slide the open jaws forward around the isolated ball, using its visible position relative to the finger tips.
